steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a programming-languages/security paper that formalizes stack safety as a set of security properties. Motivate why existing stack protections need a formal specification, describe our approach and how we validate it with random testing, and end with a contributions list and an outline of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Functions and the call stack
- Attacks on the stack and the protections against them
- Lack of formal guarantees; Lazy Tagging and Clearing as a motivating case
- Our approach: stack safety as security properties over function activations
- Why stack safety must be defined relative to features
- Validation by random testing; contributions; paper roadmap and artifact

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Functions and the call stack
  - functions/procedures/methods: units of computation invoking each other, modular
  - low level: each activation manages locals, spilled temporaries, info about caller to return to
  - call stack = fundamental data structure for functions; ABI defines how registers shared between activations
- Attacks and protections
  - attacks on stack = attacks on function abstraction itself
  - stack: ancient and perennial target (cite); control-flow hijacking via return address, or memory corruption generally
  - protections: stack canaries, bounds checking, split stacks, shadow stacks, capabilities, hardware tagging (cite each)
  - enforcement brittle: stop one attack, leave others; "whack-a-mole"
  - want formal properties of safe behavior, proven or rigorously tested; spec to validate enforcement against; even failing mechanisms benefit from saying why/when they fail
- Lack of formal guarantees
  - many mechanisms ill-suited: impede attackers, no universal protection
  - shadow stacks: quote "restrict the flexibility available in creating gadget chains" (cite)
  - SoftBound, code-pointer integrity: stronger but not formal guarantees
  - only formal line: secure calling conventions, Skorstengaard et al. and Georges et al.
  - Roessler and DeHon: tag-based micro-policies for stack safety, aim for universal protection
  - optimizations Lazy Tagging and Lazy Clearing, deployed together -> LTC
  - LTC lets activations write into each other's frames, but owner can't access corrupted memory afterward; avoids expensive clearing
  - corruption allowed, just not observable -> fails Georges et al.'s property (tagged setting), but arguably stack safe: data-flow integrity tied to stack
  - need looser, more observational definition
- Our approach
  - protect function activations from each other; language-based security; activations as security principals
  - family of properties: integrity + confidentiality of caller's local state and callee's behavior during/after callee, plus well-bracketed control flow (WBCF) from Skorstengaard et al.
- Feature-relative definition
  - stated abstractly, hope to apply beyond LTC; no universal definition for all architectures/compilers
  - can't define purely at source level + secure compiler: "the stack" implicit in calls/returns
  - can't define purely low-level: "well-behaved stack" almost vacuous; ISA doesn't care if caller frame readable/writable by callee
  - so: which high-level features use the stack, how do they shape WBCF, confidentiality, integrity?
  - simple system first, then realistic: tail-call elimination, stack argument passing, callee-save registers
  - five properties, same basic structure, features cause subtler differences
- Validation, contributions, roadmap
  - QuickChick, property-based random testing for Coq
  - published LTC flawed: breaks integrity and confidentiality; fixed version satisfies all
  - extend LTC for realistic system, test against extended properties
  - contributions: (1) stack safety = conjunction of confidentiality/integrity for callee and caller + WBCF, parameterized over external observation, covers lazy enforcement; (2) extension: stack args, callee-saves, tail calls, modular; (3) validate LTC by testing, find flaw, fix
  - sections: overview; III example walkthrough; IV formal model; V extended features; VII micro-policies; VIII testing; IX, X related/future work
  - artifact: Coq definitions + testing framework, no proofs; Coq used for QuickChick and unambiguous definitions; proofs future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Functions in high-level languages (and similar abstractions like procedures and methods) are units of computation that call each other so that larger computations can be built in a modular way. At the low level, each function activation manages its own local variables and spilled temporaries, and also information about the caller it will return to. The call stack is the basic data structure that is used to implement functions, together with an Application Binary Interface (ABI) which defines how the registers are shared between activations.

From the security point of view, an attack on the call stack is an attack on the function abstraction itself. The stack has been a target for low-level attacks for a very long time and it still is. Sometimes the attacks hijack control flow by corrupting the return address, and sometimes they corrupt memory more generally.

There are as many protections as there are attacks, in software and in hardware: stack canaries, bounds checking, split stacks, shadow stacks, capabilities, and hardware tagging. But enforcement mechanisms can be brittle, and they can stop one attack but leave room for another one. We don't want to play whack-a-mole forever, so we want formal properties of safe behavior that can be proven, or at least tested rigorously. These properties can then be the specification that enforcement is validated against. Even an enforcement mechanism that doesn't satisfy a property benefits, because we can say why and when it can fail.

Many of these mechanisms are basically not suited to giving formal guarantees. They may make life harder for attackers, but they don't give universal protection. For example, shadow stacks aim to “restrict the flexibility available in creating gadget chains”, and not to rule out attacks categorically. Some other mechanisms, like SoftBound and code-pointer integrity, do aim for stronger guarantees, but those guarantees are not formal. As far as we know, the only line of work that makes a formal claim to protect stack safety is the work on secure calling conventions by Skorstengaard et al. and Georges et al..

- Some other mechanisms should also allow strong formal guarantees
  - Roessler and DeHon: tag-based micro-policies for stack safety aiming at universal protection
  - subtle reasoning: Lazy Tagging and Lazy Clearing, deployed together = LTC
  - LTC: activations can write into each other's frames improperly, but owner cannot access corrupted memory afterward; avoids expensive frame clearing
  - corruption allowed but not observable -> fails Georges et al.'s property (tagged setting); still arguably stack safety (data-flow integrity tied to stack)
  - need a looser, more observational definition
- Our approach: protect activations from each other, language-based security, activations as security principals
  - integrity/confidentiality of caller's local state and callee's behavior during and after the call + WBCF (Skorstengaard et al.)
- Abstract statement, but no universal definition
  - not purely source-level (stack implicit in calls/returns); not purely low-level (almost vacuous; ISA doesn't care)
  - which high-level features use the stack and how they affect WBCF, confidentiality, integrity
  - simple system, then tail-call elimination, stack arguments, callee-save registers; five properties keep their structure
- Testing with QuickChick (Coq): published LTC flawed (integrity + confidentiality); fixed version passes; extended LTC tested against extended properties
- Contributions (3 bullets), section roadmap, Coq artifact without proofs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Functions in high-level languages (and similar abstractions like procedures and methods) are units of computation that call each other so that larger computations can be built in a modular way. At the low level, each function activation manages its own local variables and spilled temporaries, and also information about the caller it will return to. The call stack is the basic data structure that is used to implement functions, together with an Application Binary Interface (ABI) which defines how the registers are shared between activations.

From the security point of view, an attack on the call stack is an attack on the function abstraction itself. The stack has been a target for low-level attacks for a very long time and it still is. Sometimes the attacks hijack control flow by corrupting the return address, and sometimes they corrupt memory more generally.

There are as many protections as there are attacks, in software and in hardware: stack canaries, bounds checking, split stacks, shadow stacks, capabilities, and hardware tagging. But enforcement mechanisms can be brittle, and they can stop one attack but leave room for another one. We don't want to play whack-a-mole forever, so we want formal properties of safe behavior that can be proven, or at least tested rigorously. These properties can then be the specification that enforcement is validated against. Even an enforcement mechanism that doesn't satisfy a property benefits, because we can say why and when it can fail.

Many of these mechanisms are basically not suited to giving formal guarantees. They may make life harder for attackers, but they don't give universal protection. For example, shadow stacks aim to “restrict the flexibility available in creating gadget chains”, and not to rule out attacks categorically. Some other mechanisms, like SoftBound and code-pointer integrity, do aim for stronger guarantees, but those guarantees are not formal. As far as we know, the only line of work that makes a formal claim to protect stack safety is the work on secure calling conventions by Skorstengaard et al. and Georges et al..

Some of the other mechanisms should also be able to get strong formal guarantees. In particular, Roessler and DeHon present a set of tag-based micro-policies for stack safety which aim to give universal protection. But the reasoning is subtle. They include micro-policy optimizations called Lazy Tagging and Lazy Clearing, which would probably be deployed together, so we call them Lazy Tagging and Clearing, or LTC. LTC lets function activations write improperly into each other's stack frames, but it makes sure that the owner of the corrupted memory cannot access it afterwards, and this avoids expensive clearing of the stack frame. So under this policy one activation can corrupt the memory of another one, just not in a way that affects observable behavior. This means LTC would not satisfy Georges et al.'s property (if it was adapted to the tagged setting). But LTC arguably does enforce stack safety, or what Roessler and DeHon informally describe as a kind of data-flow integrity tied to the stack. To fit this situation we need a looser and more observational definition of stack safety.

In this paper we propose a formal characterization of stack safety. It is based on the intuition that function activations should be protected from each other, and it uses the tools of language-based security to treat function activations as security principals. We decompose stack safety into a family of properties. These describe integrity and confidentiality of the caller's local state and of the callee's behavior during (and after) the execution of the callee, together with the well-bracketed control flow (WBCF) property described by Skorstengaard et al..

We state our properties abstractly, hoping that they can be applied to other enforcement mechanisms and not only LTC. However, it doesn't seem feasible to give one universal definition of stack safety for all architectures and compilers. Many security properties can be described just at the level of a high-level programming language and then translated to a target machine by a secure compiler, but stack safety can't be defined like this, because "the stack" is not explicitly there in the definitions of most source languages, it is implicit in the semantics of features such as calls and returns. But stack safety also can't be described coherently as a purely low-level property. At the lowest level, the specification of a "well-behaved stack" is almost vacuous. The ISA doesn't care about questions like whether a callee should be able to read or write its caller's frame. Those questions belong to the high-level languages that are built on top of the hardware stack.

So any low-level treatment of stack safety has to start by asking which high-level features are supported using the stack in a given setting, and how their presence influences what we expect for well-bracketed control flow, confidentiality and integrity. We start with a simple system that has very few features and then move to a more realistic one, which supports tail-call elimination, argument passing on the stack, and callee-save registers. The properties are factored so that the basic structure of each of our five properties stays the same, and the presence or absence of the different features leads to subtler differences in how they behave.

We show that our properties are useful for telling correct and incorrect enforcement apart by using QuickChick, which is a property-based random testing tool for Coq. In fact, we find that the published version of LTC has a flaw that undermines both integrity and confidentiality. After we correct the flaw, LTC satisfies all our properties. We also modify LTC to protect the features of the more realistic system, and we use random testing to validate this extended mechanism against the extended properties.

To summarize, our contributions are:

- We give a new characterization of stack safety as a conjunction of security properties (confidentiality and integrity for callee and caller) plus well-bracketed control flow. The properties are parameterized over a notion of external observation, which lets them characterize lazy enforcement mechanisms.

- We extend these core definitions to a realistic setting with argument passing on the stack, callee-saves registers, and tail-call elimination. The model is modular enough that adding these features is straightforward.

- We validate a published enforcement mechanism, Lazy Tagging and Clearing, with property-based random testing, find that it falls short, and propose and validate a fix.

The next section gives a short overview of our framework and assumptions. Section III goes through a function call in a simple example machine, discusses informally how each property applies to it, and motivates the properties from a security point of view. Section IV formalizes the machine model, its security semantics, and the stack safety properties that are built on them. Section V describes how to support an extended set of features. Section VII describes the micro-policies we test, Section VIII the testing framework itself, and Sections IX and X related and future work.

The accompanying artifact contains the formal definitions (in Coq) of our properties and our testing framework. There are no proofs in it, since we use Coq mainly for the QuickChick testing library and to make sure our definitions are unambiguous. Formal proofs are left as future work.

steps.text:
Functions in high-level languages (and related abstractions such as procedures and methods) are units of computation that invoke one another to define larger computations in a modular way. At a low level, each function activation manages its own local variables, spilled temporaries, etc., as well as information about the caller to which it will return. The call stack is the fundamental data structure used to implement functions, aided by an Application Binary Interface (ABI) that defines how registers are shared between activations.

From a security perspective, attacks on the call stack are attacks on the function abstraction itself. Indeed, the stack is an ancient [1] and perennial [2,3,4,5,6,7] target for low-level attacks, sometimes involving control-flow hijacking by corrupting the return address, sometimes memory corruption more generally.

The variety of attacks on the stack is matched by the range of software and hardware protections that aim to prevent them, including stack canaries [8], bounds checking [9,10,11], split stacks [12], shadow stacks [13,14], capabilities [15,16,17,18,19], and hardware tagging [20,21]. But enforcement mechanisms can be brittle, eliminating one attack while leaving room for others. To avoid an endless game of whack-a-mole, we want formal properties of safe behavior that can be proven, or at least rigorously tested. Such properties can serve as the specification against which enforcement is validated—even mechanisms that do not fulfill a property benefit from being able to say why and when they may fail.

Many of the mechanisms above are fundamentally ill-suited to offering formal guarantees: they may impede attackers, but they do not provide universal protection. Shadow stacks, for instance, aim to “restrict the flexibility available in creating gadget chains” [14], not to categorically rule out attacks. Other mechanisms, such as SoftBound [9] and code-pointer integrity [12], do aim for stronger guarantees, but not formal ones. To our knowledge, the only line of work making a formal claim to protect stack safety is the study of secure calling conventions by Skorstengaard et al. [18] and Georges et al. [19].

Some of the other mechanisms listed above should also be amenable to strong formal guarantees. In particular, Roessler and DeHon [20] present a set of tag-based micro-policies [22] for stack safety that aim to offer universal protection. But the reasoning involved is subtle: they include micro-policy optimizations, Lazy Tagging and Lazy Clearing (likely deployed together, which we refer to as Lazy Tagging and Clearing, or LTC). LTC allows function activations to write improperly into one another’s stack frames, but ensures that the owner of the corrupted memory cannot access it afterward, avoiding expensive clearing of the stack frame. Under this policy, one activation can corrupt another’s memory—just not in ways that affect observable behavior. LTC would therefore not fulfill Georges et al.’s property (adapted to the tagged setting). Yet LTC arguably does enforce stack safety, or, as Roessler and DeHon informally describe it, a sort of data-flow integrity tied to the stack. Fitting this situation requires a looser, more observational definition of stack safety.

We propose here a formal characterization of stack safety based on the intuition of protecting function activations from each other, using the tools of language-based security [23] to treat function activations as security principals. We decompose stack safety into a family of properties describing the integrity and confidentiality of the caller’s local state and of the callee’s behavior during (and after) the callee’s execution, together with the well-bracketed control flow (WBCF) property articulated by Skorstengaard et al. [18].

Our properties are stated abstractly in the hope that they can be applied to enforcement mechanisms other than LTC. However, a universal definition of stack safety that applies to all architectures and compilers does not seem feasible. Many security properties can be described purely at the level of a high-level language and carried to a target machine by a secure compiler, but stack safety cannot be defined this way, since “the stack” is not explicitly present in the definitions of most source languages; it is implicit in the semantics of features such as calls and returns. Nor can stack safety be described coherently as a purely low-level property: at the lowest level, the specification of a “well-behaved stack” is almost vacuous. The ISA is not concerned with whether a caller’s frame should be readable or writable by its callee. Such questions are the purview of the high-level languages built atop the hardware stack.

Any low-level treatment of stack safety must therefore begin by asking which high-level features are supported using the stack in a given setting, and how their presence influences the expectations of well-bracketed control flow, confidentiality, and integrity. We begin with a simple system with very few features, then move to a more realistic one supporting tail-call elimination, argument passing on the stack, and callee-save registers. Our properties are factored so that the basic structure of each of our five properties stays constant, while the presence or absence of different features leads to subtler differences in how they behave.

We demonstrate that our properties are useful for distinguishing correct from incorrect enforcement using QuickChick [25,26], a property-based random testing tool for Coq. We find that the published version of LTC is flawed in a way that undermines both integrity and confidentiality; once this flaw is corrected, LTC satisfies all of our properties. We further modify LTC to protect the features of our more realistic system and use random testing to validate this extended mechanism against the extended properties.

In summary, we offer the following contributions:

- • We give a novel characterization of stack safety as a conjunction of security properties—confidentiality and integrity for callee and caller—plus well-bracketed control flow. The properties are parameterized over a notion of external observation, which allows them to characterize lazy enforcement mechanisms.

- • We extend these core definitions to a realistic setting with argument passing on the stack, callee-saves registers, and tail-call elimination. The model is modular enough that adding these features is straightforward.

- • We validate a published enforcement mechanism, Lazy Tagging and Clearing, via property-based random testing, find that it falls short, and propose and validate a fix.

The following section gives a brief overview of our framework and assumptions. Section III walks through a function call in a simple example machine, discusses informally how each property applies to it, and motivates the properties from a security perspective. Section IV formalizes the machine model, its security semantics, and the stack safety properties built on them. Section V describes how to support an extended set of features. Section VII describes the micro-policies we test, Section VIII the testing framework itself, and Sections IX and X related and future work.

The accompanying artifact contains formal definitions (in Coq) of our properties, along with our testing framework. It does not include proofs, since we use Coq mainly for the QuickChick testing library and to make sure our definitions are unambiguous. Formal proofs are left as future work.
